title: How do retries and circuit breakers make a system resilient?
description: Transient-fault handling: retry policies with backoff and jitter, circuit breaker states, bulkheads, and why naive retries make outages worse.

data.text: **Question:** How do retries and circuit breakers make a system resilient?

**Retries** turn transient failures (a blip, a timed-out socket, a 503) into apparent success — but only when combined with **exponential backoff + jitter** and a cap, or a full-outage retry storm turns a small problem into a self-inflicted DoS. A **circuit breaker** stops calling a failing dependency after a failure threshold, fails fast for a cool-down period, then lets a **half-open probe** through to test recovery — protecting your service's threads/timeouts from waiting on a dead dependency and giving it room to recover. Together with **timeouts** (the foundation — no retry without a tight timeout) and **bulkheads** (isolated thread pools/connection limits per dependency), they implement the Bulkhead + Circuit Breaker + Retry trio from the Netflix/Polly resilience toolkit. In .NET: **Polly** (now Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience) gives you all of it declaratively.

**Retry done right:**
- **Timeout first**: a hung dependency without a timeout never fails, so it never retries — it just exhausts your threads
- Retry only **retryable** conditions: network faults, 503/429, timeouts. NOT 400/401/404 — retrying a validation error is noise
- **Exponential backoff with jitter**: 100ms → 200ms → 400ms, plus random jitter so a thousand clients don't retry in lockstep
- Cap attempts (2–3 for user-facing paths) and cap total time (budget: the user isn't waiting 30s)
- Retries must be **idempotent** on the server side (see idempotency lesson) — a timed-out-but-succeeded request retried is a duplicate charge

**Circuit breaker mechanics:**
- **Closed**: normal; failures counted against a threshold (e.g., 50% of 20 calls in 10s)
- **Open**: calls fail fast immediately (throw/fallback) for the cool-down — the dependency gets breathing room, your request threads stop piling up
- **Half-open**: allow a few probe calls; success closes the breaker, failure re-opens with backoff
- Trip on the right signals: timeouts and 5xx, not 4xx

**Bulkheads:**
- Separate thread pools/connection limits per dependency — one slow third-party can't consume every thread
- Bulkhead + breaker together: even in the open state, some threads are reserved for probes

**The composed picture:** tight timeout → retry with backoff/jitter for idempotent calls → breaker around the whole thing → bulkhead isolating it → fallback (cached value, degraded response, queue-and-replay) so users still get something

**.NET specifics:** Polly policies (Retry, CircuitBreaker, Timeout, Bulkhead) via Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience/Http; standard resilience handler on HttpClient; Azure SDKs ship built-in retry policies (respect Retry-After on 429)

data.title: A composed resilience pipeline in .NET
Retries amplify outages
data.text: Without jitter and caps, every client retries the same dependency at the same moments — turning a 10-second blip into a load spike that finishes the job. When the dependency is *your own service*, retries across clients with synchronized backoff are a classic self-inflicted incident. Jitter is not optional.

items: Retrying without timeouts — a hung call never fails, so it never retries
Retrying non-idempotent operations — duplicate side effects
No jitter or backoff — synchronized retry storms
Retrying 4xx client errors — pointless load, delayed feedback
Breaker with no fallback — users get raw exceptions when it opens (degrade deliberately)
One global retry policy for all dependencies — the slow analytics API shouldn't share the payment path's budget
How do you pick failure thresholds and break durations in practice?
How does Retry-After on 429 change the retry strategy?
Where do bulkheads fit relative to the breaker?
How do you test resilience policies — does Polly have a chaos story?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Timeout → retry (backoff + jitter, transient-only, capped) → breaker → bulkhead → fallback
Breaker states: closed → open (fail fast) → half-open (probe) → closed
Pipelines are per-dependency: budgets differ by criticality
data.takeaway: Resilience is layered: retries absorb blips, breakers stop the bleeding, bulkheads contain it — and jitter keeps your retries from becoming the outage.
